title: I'm making a thrift-shop game with AI help. Do the repair choices come across in this clip?
author: huevanwang
selftext:
Here's the current loop in Thrift Hunter, a little secondhand-shop game I'm making in Godot. You buy an old object, work out what's wrong with it, fix it with tool cards and repair processes, then choose a buyer. A few finds have engravings or recordings that open up a story.

I'm using Codex to help with code and this edit, plus generative tools for some background/UI art. This is a recording of the actual game. The dialogue is prewritten; the game doesn't call an AI while you play.

The awkward bit has been turning a working system into something pleasant to play. At one point, every tiny repair task used up a whole work round. There was too much stopping and starting. I've been cutting that down and letting smaller jobs share a round.

What I'm aiming for is a small decision with each find: is this worth fixing, should I preserve its original parts, and when should I stop? I'm less sure whether the cards help communicate that.

Do the cards feel like a useful way to plan the repair, or does the 3D object make you expect to work on it more directly? I'd especially like to hear where the clip becomes hard to follow. A timestamp is plenty.
